title: 4. Week 4 - Hypothesis testing, significance testing
text:
Lectures
Last week, we explored how two measures can vary together. You practised visualising the relationship using scatterplots and estimating Pearson’s \(r\). We also talked about how we respect participants’ choices, collect and protect appropriate data, and interpret and communicate research findings responsibly.
This week, we learn about hypothesis testing and significance testing and apply this to correlation analysis. We will also practise reporting correlation analysis following APA conventions.
We will make a start with the group project.






Important



Please watch the lecture material, complete the essential reading and then the pre-lab activities before attending your lab. As a reminder, the lectures and pre-labs introduce the concepts and give you some initial practice, and the lab gives you the opportunity to apply these skills in-person with our support.








Questions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Hypothesis testing, significance testing
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Our lecture on hypothesis testing and significance testing, shown next, is split into six short parts that you should watch in sequence.


1. Hypothesis testing and significance testing (~70 minutes in total)
You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.
The slides end with a references list but don’t worry about reading what’s in the references list, we give you recommended readings in Section 2.






Tip



The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: hypothesis-testing-significance.html.

Lecture slides

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.
There are many slides but not all slides are discussed in-depth in the lecture, some are there to help to visually support transitions between points.


Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in the order they are shown in.
1.1. We are going to learn about hypothesis or significance testing (~5 minutes). This is a challenging topic. We can meet this challenge by enriching our perspectives to take in historical, philosophical, and psychological viewpoints.

    

1.2. What is NHST and where does it come from? (~13 minutes). We are going to learn about hypothesis testing and significance from two different perspectives: (1.) The perspective of an individual researcher, asking what they can learn from the evidence from their study. (2.) The perspective of someone looking at errors that we (in general) could make as we make decisions based on the evidence from multiple repeated studies. We begin with the first perspective, based on Ronald Fisher’s ideas.

    

1.3. Demonstration: significance testing (~20 minutes). We have outlined the logic of the significance test in words. But it is often easier to understand the logic if we see how the ideas work in practice.

    

1.4. Hypothesis testing (~10 minutes). We switch to a different philosophy and a different view of the psychology of researchers. We take a second perspective, grounded in thinking about error rates, based on the ideas of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson.

    

1.5. Seeing the Neyman-Pearson approach at work (24 minutes). To help us to build understanding, we work through demonstrations that build on realistic simulations of the kind of evidence we collect in psychological studies of correlation.

    

1.6. Summary (8 minutes). Two ways of thinking clearly about evidence. The impacts on how we write about and think about research as psychologists.

    














Take a break!



Before continuing, we recommend you take a 15-minute break away from your computer. Remember to note down any questions to bring to the Q&A, lab or discussion forum whilst you’re watching the lectures.

text:
Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
These short activities will help you to connect Week 4’s emphasis on estimating correlations with sample data in R to this week’s work on hypothesis testing and significance.






Tip



Information on the pre-lab activities will follow soon.



Pre-lab activity 1: Visualising correlations interactively
Last week, we worked on how you can examine the potential associations between variables:

visualizing potential associations between variables using scatterplots;
estimating the associations as correlations \(r\).

We showed you a couple of web apps you can use to visualize potential associations. We add a new one for this week.






Tip



Make sure you have tried these apps out.

The purpose of playing with these apps is quite serious: you are training your visualization skills, and tuning your intuitions. The only way to do this is by looking at lots of plots.




Have a look at this visualisation of correlations by Kristoffer Magnusson.

After having read the relevant sections of Howell (2017) Chapter 9 (see under Reading), use this visualisation page to visually replicate the scatterplots in Figures 9.1 and 9.2 - use a sample of 100. After that, visually replicate the scatterplots in Figure 9.3.
Each time you change the correlation, pay attention to the shared variance (the overlap between the two variables, based on R²) and see how this changes with the changing level of relationship between the two variables. The greater the shared variance, the stronger the relationship.
Also, try setting the correlation to r = .5 and then moving a single dot to see how one data point, a potential outlier, can change the stated correlation value between two variables.

Try the online app on guessing the correlation.

This allows you to see how accurately you can estimate r (correlation strengths) from a scatterplot. Click on “Track Performance” first so you can keep an overview of your overall bias to underestimate or overestimate the strength of a correlation.

New: Try this Guessing correlation coefficients app because it doesn’t hurt to look at a different kind of app.

text:
Lab activities




Lab activity 1: Finish lab activities from previous weeks (Recap - skip if completed successfully last week)

Background
Over the past few weeks, we worked with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering. You can have a look at the questionnaire here.
If you did not successfully finish the lab activities for weeks 1, 2 or 3, you may want to complete these first.
You can log into the R server, open your project (the .Rproj file) and open the Quarto file (ending with .qmd) to continue to work through these.


Aims of the activity
Ensure you are familiar with reading in a .csv-file, creating a histogram and calculating summary statistics.


Steps

Login to the R-server
Click on the R-project (the Rproj) file to open it
In the Files tab (right bottom quadrant), navigate to the example script for that week’s lab activities. This is the Quarto file (ending with .qmd). Click on it to open it.
Complete any remaining activities




Lab activity 2: Hypothesis testing for correlations – getting ready

Background
This week, we are going to work with data that we have generated (through simulations) but which are based on data from a real project looking at how psychologists measure vocabulary knowledge.
Hanke Vermeiren and colleagues (Vermeiren et al., 2023) completed a series of studies to develop a vocabulary test for English-speaking university students. Among the tests they developed were measures of vocabulary knowledge (what you know about word meanings) and of reading experience (print exposure, based on recognition of author names). They share information on the tests through the repository: https://osf.io/ef3s4/overview.






Tip



I talk about this study in the lecture on Hypothesis testing, significance testing because there are good reasons to think we might see correlations between measures of vocabulary knowledge and measures of reading experience.


Reference
Vermeiren, H., Vandendaele, A., & Brysbaert, M. (2023). Validated tests for language research with university students whose native language is English: Tests of vocabulary, general knowledge, author recognition, and reading comprehension. Behavior Research Methods, 55(3), 1036–1068. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01856-x.


Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Download and organise your files
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data
Build scatterplots with geom_point() and edit your code to change how the plot looks
Calculate and interpret significance tests for correlation when you use correlation().



Download the files
To complete this lab activity you will need four files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk4_lab.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We need data files called:


correlation-data-n030.csv
correlation-data-n100.csv
correlation-data-n1000.csv

These files all hold scores on tests of vocabulary knowledge or of reading experience.

Different (simulated) participants’ scores are on different rows of each spreadsheet.
Different kinds of scores are in different columns of each spreadsheet.

Column names are shown at the top of the columns. The names encode information about what the column data are about in a [..].[..].[..].[..] four-part naming scheme:

[what test? vocabulary or experience].[is r positive or negative or zero?].[is r large, medium, small in size?].[how big is the participant sample? small (30) medium (100) large (1000)]







Click here for examples of column names





The columns have names that look like this (from correlation-data-n100.csv):

vocab.neg.lar.med – vocabulary.negative.large.medium
exper.neg.lar.med – experience.negative.large.medium
vocab.neg.med.med – vocabulary.negative.medium.medium
exper.neg.med.med – experience.negative.medium.medium
vocab.neg.sma.med – vocabulary.negative.small.medium
exper.neg.sma.med – experience.negative.small.medium
vocab.zer.zer.med – vocabulary.zero.zero.medium

exper.zer.zer.med – experience.zero.zero.medium
vocab.pos.sma.med – vocabulary.positive.large.medium
exper.pos.sma.med – experience.positive.large.medium
vocab.pos.med.med – vocabulary.positive.medium.medium

exper.pos.med.med – experience.positive.medium.medium
vocab.pos.lar.med – vocabulary.positive.small.medium
exper.pos.lar.med – experience.positive.small.medium




You can download the files here: 4141_wk4_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.
Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server: Look at bottom right quadrant of the R-server web window. There is no need to extract the files first.
Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called 4141_wk4_lab.qmd in the Files space on the R-server.






Tip



From now on, you’ll be working in RStudio.





Lab activity 3: Beautifying scatterplots

Information
We begin by working on edits to change or improve the look of your scatterplots.
You will often need to change things like:
The colour of points








Figure 1: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in colour











Click here to see how to change the colour of points





The important change is to add colour: geom_point(colour = ...)

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(colour = "limegreen") +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()




The size of points








Figure 2: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in size











Click here to see how to change the size of points





The important change is to add size: geom_point(size = ...)

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()




The transparency of points








Figure 3: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in transparency











Click here to see how to change the alpha of points





The important change is to add alpha: geom_point(alpha = ...) – alpha is how you define how dark (fractions closer to 1) or transparent points are (values closer to 0)

thirty.large <- ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = .25) +
  labs(x = "experience", y = "vocabulary") +
  theme_bw()










Tip



You often need to style plots so they are consistent with the look and feel you want for your business, your group or your self.

Here, we will need to work transparency (coding alpha) because varying transparency of points allows us to deal with over-plotting if there are lots of data points; this is when many points are printed on top of each other and things look crowded.





Question 1
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.pos.sma.sma and exper.pos.sma.sma. Make the points really big.















Question 2
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.pos.lar.sma and exper.pos.lar.sma. Make the points really colourful: whatever colour you like.















Question 3
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.neg.med.sma and exper.neg.med.sma. Make the points semi-transparent: whatever level of alpha you like.















Question 4
Create a scatterplot of the potential association in the correlation-data-n030.csv data between the variables: vocab.neg.lar.sma and exper.neg.lar.sma. Change the colour, size and transparency of the points all at the same time.















Tips: Where to find further information






Further information





1. General advice
You can find guidance on anything you want to do in R by typing words like ggplot2 reference guide geom_point. That kind of search will get you a webpage like:
https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_point.html#ref-examples

where you can find examples of code for doing things. Usually, you can scroll through the examples to find a match for what you want to achieve, and then adapt the code to your own situation.

2. Find out about colour
There are lots of guide to colour, here’s one:
https://r-graph-gallery.com/ggplot2-color.html





Answers
The answers to the questions will be available after the final lab session has taken place.



Lab activity 4: Testing and interpreting correlations
Now we are going to put the skills you have been learning together so that you can:

visualize an association between two variables;
estimate the correlation \(r\) between the two variables;
test the significance of the correlation.







Tip



What we are doing when we do significance testing is explained in the lectures. Watch the videos and come back if you have not done this already.














Use the correlation-data-n030.csv data: you will have given the data a name when you read it in using read_csv(), use that name when you do your coding.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.pos.med.sma and exper.pos.med.sma.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.pos.med.sma and exper.pos.med.sma?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?
Describe the direction of the correlation.
Is the correlation significant? Why?































Use the correlation-data-n030.csv data.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.zer.zer.sma and exper.zer.zer.sma.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.zer.zer.sma and exper.zer.zer.sma?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?
Describe the direction of the correlation.
Is the correlation significant? Why?































Now use the correlation-data-n100.csv data: you will have given the data a name when you read it in using read_csv(), use that name when you do your coding.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.pos.sma.med and exper.pos.sma.med.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.pos.sma.med and exper.pos.sma.med?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?
Describe the direction of the correlation.
Is the correlation significant? Why?































Now use the correlation-data-n1000.csv data: you will have given the data a name when you read it in using read_csv(), use that name when you do your coding.


Produce a scatterplot of the association between the variables: vocab.neg.lar.lar and exper.neg.lar.lar.
What is the correlation \(r\) between the variables: vocab.neg.lar.lar and exper.neg.lar.lar?
What are the statistics: \(r, t, p\)?
Describe the direction of the correlation.
Is the correlation significant? Why?































Answers
The answers to the questions will be available after the final lab session has taken place.



Lab activity 5: Critical reflections
We created a Shiny web app so that you can reflect critically on some of the ideas we discussed in the lecture, and that you can see play out in the exercises you have just done.






Access the app here



Access the app by clicking on this link
The app works in Chrome but not (yet) in Safari. It is under development.
You can copy the link https://robayedavies.github.io/teaching-nhst-corr-demo-shiny/ and paste it into Chrome to access the app there, if you are not already using Chrome.
Paste the link into Chrome, or click to access (if you are already working in Chrome), wait a few seconds, and you should see a webpage somewhat like the image shown next.





A shiny web app for exploring correlations


The app allows you to control:

The number of people tested: Participants per study (N) button.
The correlation: Population correlation (r) slider.
You can get new samples as many time as you like: Draw new samples button.







Tip



What we are doing when we do significance testing is explained in the lectures. Watch the videos and come back if you have not done this already.

The Our observed dataset on the left shows a single simulated dataset with the correlation and the participant sample you selected.
The Six more datasets in the middle show six further datasets with the same correlation, but each shows how the correlation can vary, given different random samples of data.


These datasets are simulated every time you click on the Participants per study (N) button or move the Population correlation (r) slider button to a new correlation value.
You can also get new simulations each time you click on the Draw new samples button (see top right of the webpage.)


The piles-of-dots on the top right of the web page show comparisons between the \(r\) correlation for Our observed dataset and distributions of \(r\) correlations for (2.) lots of samples, taken at random, assuming the null hypothesis H0 is true.
The piles-of-dots on the bottom right of the web page show comparisons between the \(r\) correlation for the “observed” dataset and distributions of \(r\) correlations for (2.) lots of samples, taken at random, assuming the alternative hypothesis HA is true.

Have a play with the web app and then answer the following questions.



Pick any correlation value using the Population correlation (r) slider. Compare the scatterplot for 1. Our observed dataset with the six scatterplots for 2. Six more datasets, same population. Look at the plots and compare:


the scatter (spread) of points
the trend shown by the points (are high experience values associated with high vocabulary scores, or not).

Here’s the question for reflection: What does this comparison tell you about the ways in which things like association vary between different samples of people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.









Keeping the correlation value you selected, click on the Draw new samples button a few times.

(i.) Look at the plots every time you do this and compare:

the scatter (spread) of points
the trend shown by the points.

(ii.) Also, look at the pile-of-dots plots on the right of the screen. Notice the red line move about every time you click on the Draw new samples button.

The red line indicates the r correlation estimated for the 1. Our observed dataset sample.

Here’s the question for reflection: What does this comparison tell you about the ways in which things like association vary between different samples of people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.









Now select a correlation of 0 by moving the Population correlation (r) slider, and click on the Draw new samples button a few times. Keep looking at the scatterplots and at r correlation and t (t-test statistic) values shown above the plots.


Note that if \(t > 2\) (roughly) we may expect the test statistic to be significant.

Here’s the question for reflection: We know for a fact that there is no true correlation in the population because we set the correlation value ourselves. What do the simulations suggest about what we may observe nevertheless in the samples we collect when we test people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.










Now it’s time to see what happens when we vary the size of our sample. Keep the population correlation value the same: pick any correlation you like. For this exercise, a value of \(r = .30\) is illustrative. Now click on the Participants per study (N) button to reveal a drop down menu. Choose a sample size. Try this a few times: increase the sample size up to 1000. Look at three things:


Look at the scatter of points in each scatterplot;
Look at the \(r, t, p\) statistics above each plot;
Look at the pile-of-dots plots, both the piles themselves (the shape or spread of the pile) and the red line marking the observed r.

There is a lot going on but we can pick out the key insights.
Here are the questions for reflection:

You selected the correlation value yourself, so you know what the correlation should be in the different samples: what do you see?
I expect you will see the correlation values will vary across samples (as we have seen already): what happens to this variation when you go from smaller to larger samples?
How does the per-sample correlation compare to the population correlation you selected?
What do you see happen to the piles-of-dots?

Discuss your answers with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.

title: 2. Week 2 - Measuring, describing, and visualising psychological concepts
text:
Lectures
Last week, you looked at some of the bigger questions that sit behind psychological science: how theories are linked to observable evidence, why our observations provide estimates rather than direct access to the “truth”, and why the complexity and variability of human behaviour matter.
This week, we move from those ideas to some of the practical tools that allow us to gather and make sense of evidence. We’ll look at how psychological concepts can be represented as data, and how choices about measurement, summary and visualisation shape the evidence we use to evaluate scientific claims.
The lectures are grouped into section A and B (relating to the two strands of learning stated above). Each section is split into short videos so you can work through them at your own pace. It’s a good idea to take notes as you go and to have a 10-minute break between section A and section B.






A note about the recordings



The recordings were originally delivered by Prof John Towse and have been selected and reorganised for this week’s teaching. If you hear references to a different week or to something covered “last week” don’t worry about these references! I’ve reviewed the materials and you will never be expected to know anything that you haven’t yet covered. All questions should be posted on the discussion forum and will be answered by Carly. Please do not contact John about his content.








Questions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Psychological measurement and central tendency
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Section A is broken into three parts that should be watched in sequence:

Types of data
Scales of measurement
Central tendency and notations

Download the slides for sections A and B in one go here. The transcript for all the videos is here.






Downloading files



If the file doesn’t download when you click on it, try right-clicking on it instead. You should than see multiple options and you can select ‘Download linked file’.


1. Types of data (~10 minutes)
What types of data can we use to measure psychological concepts that we are interested in? This includes nominal and numerical data.

2. Scales of Measurement (~9 minutes) Four different scales that we commonly use to measure our data. These include nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

3. Measures of central tendency and key notations (~10 minutes) Why measurement matters, and how to describe your data using numbers and appropriate measures. This includes the mean, median and mode.







Take a break!



Before continuing, we recommend you take a 15-minute break away from your computer. Remember to note down any questions to bring to the Q&A, lab or discussion forum whilst you’re watching the lectures.




Section B: Variability and distributions
Section B is broken into four parts that should be watched in sequence:

Variability in numbers
Variability in words
The standard deviation and distribution curves
The normal distribution curve

1. Variability in numbers (~19 minutes) Why does variability or ‘spread’ in our data matter? How can we measure and express variability using numbers? This includes range, interquartile range, deviance, variance and standard deviation.

2. Variability in words (~5 minutes) A short reflection on what numerical measures of variability can actually tell us about our data.







Formulae and calculations



John has just introduced the notion of using calculations to measure variability and the broader concepts behind them. You can download the key formulae for calculating variance and standard deviation and other measures here You may come across slightly different versions of these formulae (computational and conceptual) so it is useful to be aware of them. You do not need to memorise these formulae. The important thing is to understand what each measure tells us about our data and the basic idea behind how it is calculated. In the next recording, John will take you through a worked example of calculating a standard deviation.


3. The standard deviation and distribution curves (~15 minutes) An example of how to calculate standard deviation, and how we can look at variability visually using histogram plots. An overview of the shape of data distributions, with features including symmetry, skew, and bimodality.

4. The normal distribution (~9 minutes) Basic properties of the normal distribution curve and linking central tendency and standard deviation to the normal curve.

text:
Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.

Pre-lab activity 1: From psychological claims to measurements
Last week, you considered psychological claims that we might encounter in everyday life. One example is the claim that “screen time negatively impacts mental health in adolescents”. Before we could investigate this claim, we would need to decide what we actually mean by screen time and how we could turn that concept into something we can observe and measure.
One simple approach might be to ask people: “Approximately how many hours did you spend looking at a screen yesterday?”
Imagine we asked a small group of adolescents and received the following sample of responses:
6 8 5 9 7 4 11 6 7 8 10 5 6 12 7 8 4 9 6 7 14 5 8 6 10 7 3 9
Take a moment to think about what these numbers actually represent.






Pre-lab question 1




What scale of measurement best describes the number of hours of screen time reported here?



Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







Show answer





d. Ratio. Time measured in hours has equal intervals, and zero hours represents the absence of the measured quantity. This means that differences and ratios between values are meaningful.





Once we have collected observations like these, how can we describe them in a useful way? One way is to summarise the data to find the mean or average value. You’ll learn how to do that in RStudio during the lab, but for now, have a look at the website app: Describing and Exploring Quantitative Variables: https://istats.shinyapps.io/EDA_quantitative/. The website should open in a new window. You may be offered a free trial of the ‘Art of Stat Mobile App’; you can dismiss that.
Choose the following options:

Under ‘Enter Data’, select ‘Your Own’
Under ‘Name of Variable’, enter a sensible label (such as ‘Screen time’)
Under ‘Enter observations’, add the numbers of the observations
Under ‘Choose Type of Plot’, click the box to select a ‘Histogram’.

Now have a look:

On the right, you’ll see key descriptive statistics such as the mean and the standard deviation (Std. Dev.).
Below it, you can see a histogram. If the histogram looks funny, try adjusting the bin size.







What is a histogram?



A histogram is a graph that shows how the values of a continuous (or finely measured) variable are distributed. The values are divided into consecutive, equal-width intervals called bins, and a bar is drawn for each bin with its height showing how many observations fall inside it (or the proportion or density). Because the bins are adjacent, the bars touch, which distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart of separate categories. Histograms make it easy to see the shape of a distribution, including its centre, spread, skew, and any outliers or multiple peaks.


Play around:

What happens if you add more observations? How does it change the mean and the standard deviation? What happens to the histogram?
Try adding 10 observations of lower screen time values.
Try adding an impossibly large observation, like 89. That is, of course, far larger than there are hours in the day, but data entry errors like that do happen. How does it effect the mean and the standard deviation?
You can also click the option to see a boxplot as well as a histogram. Can you work out how key descriptive statistics are represented in a boxplot?







Pre-lab question 2




The mean reported screen time in this sample was approximately 7.4 hours. Which of the following would NOT be justified from these data?



Participants reported an average of 7.4 hours of screen time.
There was variation in reported screen time between participants.
Adolescents who use screens more have poorer mental health.
Some participants reported more screen time than others.







Show answer





c. Here, our measure of screen time is self-reported hours of screen use on one day. We have not measured mental health, so these observations cannot tell us whether greater screen use is associated with poorer mental health. Our measure of “screen time” is also only one possible way of representing a complex behaviour. For example, it does not distinguish between different activities or content, such as studying, gaming, messaging friends or watching videos. This illustrates an important challenge in psychological science: the questions and theories we are interested in are often complex, while the data we collect are particular observations produced by the choices we make about what and how to measure. So, even when we can accurately describe a set of observations, we still need to be careful about what those observations allow us to conclude.











Pre-lab question 3




If two sets of data have exactly the same mean, what can we conclude about their variability?



They must have the same variability
They must have the same standard deviation
One must have a larger range
We cannot tell from the mean alone







Show answer





d.

Taking part in psychological research is one of the most direct ways to understand how research works. A textbook or lecture can only take you so far. Experiencing a study from the inside shows you things that are hard to appreciate otherwise.
As a participant, you see how researchers turn abstract ideas into something measurable: how instructions are worded, how tasks are designed, how conditions are manipulated and how responses are recorded. Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
These short activities will help you connect Week 2’s emphasis on data visualisation to this week’s work with understanding relationships between two numerical variables.

Pre-lab activity 1: Why visualise data? Anscombe’s quartet
Last week, we considered the importance of visualising your data and not to just rely on the summary numbers. These measures of central tendency (e.g., mean, median, mode) are also referred to as ‘descriptive statistics’ or ‘summary statistics’. This is because we use them to summarise and describe our data, but we do not use them to make any inferences about our data.
Anscombe’s quartet (1973) showed that four different sets of bivariate data (where X and Y are both recorded for each participant) with very similar summary statistics (including means, variances and Pearson correlation coefficients) can look very different when plotted. You can read more about this and explore the four plots here.
Look closely at the plots. Which one looks approximately linear? Which shows a curved pattern? Where does a single unusual observation have a particularly strong influence?






Takeaway



A correlation coefficient is useful, but looking at a scatterplot helps us spot features that one number cannot show.




Pre-lab activity 2: Visualising correlations interactively
Have a look at this visualisation of correlations by Kristoffer Magnusson.
After having read the relevant sections of Howell (2017) Chapter 9 (see under Reading), use this visualisation page to visually replicate the scatterplots in Figures 9.1 and 9.2 - use a sample of 100. After that, visually replicate the scatterplots in Figure 9.3.
Each time you change the correlation, pay attention to the shared variance (the overlap between the two variables, based on R²) and see how this changes with the changing level of relationship between the two variables. The greater the shared variance, the stronger the relationship.
Also, try setting the correlation to r = .5 and then moving a single dot to see how one data point, a potential outlier, can change the stated correlation value between two variables.


Pre-lab activity 3: Guess the correlation
Try this online app on guessing the correlation.
This allows you to see how accurately you can estimate r (correlation strengths) from a scatterplot. Click on “Track Performance” first so you can keep an overview of your overall bias to underestimate or overestimate the strength of a correlation.
Is this all just a bit of fun? Well, yes, because stats is actually fun, and no, because it serves a purpose of helping you determine if the correlations you see in your own data are real, and to help you see if correlations in published research match with what you are being told. As you will have seen from the above examples, one data point can lead to a misleading relationship and even what might be considered a medium to strong relationship may actually have only limited relevance in the real world. It is our responsibility as psychological scientists to interpret our findings appropriately and to not overstate our results. We will think more about this in the lab this week.

FALSE Explanation: The correlation coefficient is negative and therefore infers a negative correlation. As such, older people pay less for car insurance: as age increases, car insurance costs decrease.




Suppose that there is a correlation of r = .87 between the length of time a person is in prison and the amount of aggression the person displays on a psychological inventory administered at release. This means that spending a longer amount of time in prison causes people to become more aggressive.







Answer





FALSE Explanation: This is a bit of trick question as it has the sneaky ‘cause’ word in. The correlation coefficient is a positive number, suggesting a positive relationship between length of time in prison and aggression. However, causation cannot be inferred from correlation and therefore we cannot know whether time spent in prison CAUSES aggression, and rather we suggest a relationship between the two: as length of time in prison increases, aggression increases.




A significant correlation was found between having great hair and performance in research methods and stats labs. The correlation coefficient was .7. How much variance in research methods and stats lab performance can the ‘greatness’ of your hair explain?







Answer





c 49% The ‘coefficient of determination’ or ‘R-squared’ tells us the proportion or variance in one variable that can be predicted if we know the other variable. We can determine this by squaring the r. Therefore, .72 = .49, R2 = .49.

Lab activity 3: Reminders through association
For this lab, we’re going to use data from Rogers, T. & Milkman, K. L. (2016). Reminders through association. Psychological Science, 27, 973-986. You can read the full paper online but the short version is that the authors looked at how people remember to follow through with the intention of doing something.
Although there are lots of potential reasons (e.g., some people may lack the self-control resources), Rogers and Milkman (2016) propose that some people fail to follow through simply because they forget about their good intentions. If this is the case, the authors argue, then having visual reminders to follow through on their intentions may help people remember to keep them. For example, a person may choose to put a sticker for their gym on their car window, so that every time they get in the car they remember to go to the gym.
In Study 1 by Rogers and colleagues, participants took part in an unrelated experiment but at the start of the task they were asked to return a small stack of paper clips to the reception of the building at the end of the study and if they did so the researchers would donate $1 to a charity. They were then asked if they intended to do this. Those in the reminder-through-association (RTA) condition read “Thank you! To remind you to pick up a paper clip, an elephant statuette will be sitting on the counter as you collect your payment.” This message was followed by a picture of the elephant statuette. Those in the control condition simply read “Thank you!”.
What we want to do is to run a chi-square analysis to determine whether those in the reminder-through-association condition were more likely to remember to return the paper-clips than those in the control condition.

Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data files

It is a fairly simple data file that contains four variables for 87 participants:

Questions Step 2 The numbers in the first row across the four columns refer to the responses from participant 1.

What condition were they in?
Did they intend to return the paper-clips?

Step 3: Some data wrangling - Use filter() to keep relevant data
We need to do a little bit of wrangling to get our data into the format we need: First, we need to remove all the participants who said that they did not intend to return the paper-clips (intend = 0) as we are only interested in whether people follow through on an intention.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use filter() to remove all participants who said that they did not intend to return the paper-clips. Can a look below for a reminder on how filter() works. Give it a go. If you’re stuck, have a look at the Code below.







How does filter() work?



The filter() function allows you to select specific rows from a data frame based on one or more conditions.
For example, imagine we have a dataset containing information about participants in a psychology study, including their age and gender. We might want to select only participants who are over 18 years old.
We can do this using:
filter(data, age > 18)
Here: - data is the name of our data frame. - age > 18 is the condition we want to apply. - note these two bits of information are separated within the function by a comma. - only rows where the condition is TRUE are kept.
We can also apply multiple conditions. For example, to select participants who are over 18 and identify as a woman:
filter(data, age > 18, gender == "Woman")
When we provide multiple conditions separated by commas, filter() keeps only rows that satisfy all of the conditions.
Some useful operators for filtering data include:



Operator
Meaning
Example




==
Equal to
gender == "Woman"


!=
Not equal to
gender != "Woman"


>
Greater than
age > 18


<
Less than
age < 30


>=
Greater than or equal to
age >= 18


<=
Less than or equal to
age <= 30



We can also use & (AND) and | (OR) to combine conditions.
For example:
filter(data, age >= 18 & age <= 30)
This selects participants aged between 18 and 30 (inclusive).

Step 4: Some more data wrangling - Use recode_values() to have text labels
To make the output easier to read, we’re going to recode the values for our key variables (condition and actualdonate) to have text labels rather than numerical values.
For this we can use the functions mutate() and recode_values().

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use mutate() and recode_values() to change the numerical values for condition and actualdonate to text labels. The code to do this is below. You can copy it, but have a good look to make sure you understand what each bit does.

Step 5: Descriptive statistics
Next you need to calculate descriptive statistics. For frequency data these are simply counts so we can use the function count() to do this. We want to know how many participants are in each group (rta - donated, rta - didn’t donate, control - donated, control - didn’t donate).

  percent = 100 * n / sum(n),

We want to create a simple bar plot of our count data. We’ll use ggplot() for this in combination with the geom_bar() function.

  geom_bar(position = "dodge")



Questions Step 6

What does position = "dodge" do? Remove it and rerun the code to find out.
Describe the pattern in the data in your own words.

As you can see, the plot makes it much easier to get your head around what the data mean: Participants in the RTA condition appear to have been more likely to remember to donate than those in the control condition.
The ggplot2() package allows you to customise all aspects of your plots, so let’s tidy ours up a little bit. We’re going to do the following:

Edit the labels on the x-axis, y-axis and fill
Change the colours of the bars by using scale_fill_manual() and specifying the colours we want in the values argument
Change the theme of the plot to change how it looks


Action: Copy the code below to a new code chunk. In your Quarto document, write a comment to describe what each line of code does.

ggplot(data = intent_data, aes(x = condition, fill = actualdonate)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Condition", labels = c("Control", "RTA")) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Count") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Behaviour", labels = c("Donated", "Did not donate"), values = c("blue", "grey"))+
  theme_classic()
There are a few things to note about the code we just added on:

If you use simple colour names then you are restricted in the options you can choose, however, if you want more flexibility you can use hexadecimal colour codes, see here.
There are multiple themes that you can apply. Have a look at the ggplot2() cheatsheet for an overview (here). Try out a few and see which one you prefer.



Step 7: Run the chi-square analysis
Now let’s run that chi-square analysis to see whether our impression from the plot holds up and there is a significant association between the grouping variables.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results <- chisq.test(x = intent_data$condition,
y = intent_data$actualdonate,
correct = FALSE)
results






How does chisq.test() work?



results <- chisq.test(x = intent_recode$condition,        # the first grouping variable
                      y = intent_recode$actualdonate,     # the second grouping variable
                      correct = FALSE)                    # whether we want to apply the continuity correction (use if any of the expected cell frequencies < 10 in 2 x 2 table)
results


Question Step 7: What do you conclude from the output?


Step 8: Check the assumptions
The assumptions for chi-square are as follows:

The data in the cells should be frequencies, or counts of cases rather than percentages.
The levels (or categories) of the variables are mutually exclusive. That is, a particular participant fits into one and only one group of each of the variables.
Each participant may contribute data to one and only one cell. If, for example, the same participants are tested over time such that the comparisons are of the same subjects at Time 1, Time 2, Time 3, etc., then Chi-square may not be used.
The study groups must be independent. This means that a different test must be used if the two groups are related. For example, a different test must be used if the researcher’s data consists of paired samples, such as in studies in which a parent is paired with his or her child.
There are 2 variables, and both are measured as categories, usually at the nominal level. While Chi-square has no rule about limiting the number of cells (by limiting the number of categories for each variable), a very large number of cells (over 20) can make it difficult to meet assumption #6 below, and to interpret the meaning of the results.
The expected cell frequencies should be greater than 5.

Assumptions 1) to 5) should be evaluated by reviewing the design of the study. The only assumption that we need to check with R is whether all expected frequencies are greater than 5. This information is in the object in which you stored the results of the Chi-square test, under expected.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results$expected
Question Step 8: What do you conclude from the output?


Step 9: Calculate the effect size
The last step before writing up the results is to calculate an effect size so that we have a standardised measure of how large the association between our grouping variables is. The effect size measure for chi-square is Cramer’s V. To calculate Cramer’s V we’re going to use the function cramers_v() from the easystats package. The code mirrors the code used for the Chi-square test itself.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

effect_size <- cramers_v(x = intent_data$condition,     
                         y = intent_data$actualdonate) 
effect_size
We can square the effect size (or multiple it by itself) to see how much variance in one variable is accounted for by the other variable. Use the code snippet below to square the effect size.
percentageAccountedFor <- effect_size * effect_size *100
percentageAccountedFor
Question Step 9: How large is the effect and how much variance is accounted for?


Step 10: Adjusted standardised residuals
To help interpret the relationship, it is useful to look at the adjusted standardised residuals. These are z-scores showing how many standard deviations each observed count is above or below the count expected if the variables were unrelated, so they indicate which cells differ most from expectation. Because they approximately follow a standard normal distribution, values beyond ±1.96 indicate a difference at p < .05 (two-tailed), beyond ±2.58 at p < .01, and beyond ±3.29 at p < .001.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results$residuals   # check the adjusted standardised residuals
Question Step 10: What do you conclude from the output?

Using the guidance below, have a go at writing up the results for the Chi-square analysis following APA guidelines.

1. The mini research project






Why do we do a mini research project?



Lectures and textbooks can only take you so far. Doing research shows you things that are hard to appreciate any other way.
You see how ideas become measurable. From the inside, you see how researchers turn abstract ideas into measurable variables: how instructions are worded, questions are designed and responses are recorded. You may also notice how your own expectations shape what you do. These are the issues you’ll need to think critically about in your own designs, such as demand characteristics, operationalisation and measurement validity.
You see ethics in practice. Information sheets, informed consent, the right to withdraw and debriefing make more sense once you’ve implemented them.
You see why sample size and representativeness matter. Your own research will depend on others choosing to take part, and the project gives you a first-hand sense of that.
In short, the mini project helps you become a better researcher by connecting what you learn in class to real research practice.

4. Measuring mind wandering and screen time






Important



With your group you need to decide how to measure the variables you’ve specified in your research question. In this module we focus on using questionnaires to measure constructs.
The questionnaire needs to be:

open access (that is, openly available and free to use);
accompanied by a peer-reviewed article that discusses the construction, validity and reliability of the questionnaire.

Below I’ve listed some examples, but you can propose a different questionnaire you have found in the literature as long as it satisfies the above criteria. Asking people to report (a specific aspect of) their screen-time as recorded in a screentime app is also acceptable.








Tip



Fife-Schaw, C. (2020). 14: Questionnaire design. In G. M. Breakwell, D. B. Wright, & J. Barnett (Eds.), Research methods in psychology (5th ed., pp. 119–138). SAGE Publications. Recommended

This chapter provides a useful overview of things to consider when setting up a questionnaire study.









Tip



All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow this link.


Examples of papers that discuss questionnaires that measure mind wandering
Carriere, J. S. A., Seli, P., & Smilek, D. (2013). Wandering in both mind and body: Individual differences in mind wandering and inattention predict fidgeting. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology/Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale, 67(1), 19–31. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031438

Carriere et al. (2013) capture two forms of mind wandering using the Mind Wandering: Spontaneous (MW-S) and Mind Wandering: Deliberate (MW-D) scales.

Mrazek, M. D., Phillips, D. T., Franklin, M. S., Broadway, J. M., & Schooler, J. W. (2013). Young and restless: Validation of the Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) reveals disruptive impact of mind-wandering for youth. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, Article 560. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00560

Mrazek et al. (2013) created a 5-item Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) and showed across four studies that people who score higher on it report more task-unrelated thoughts during a reading test.

Schubert, A.-L., Frischkorn, G. T., Sadus, K., Welhaf, M. S., Kane, M. J., & Rummel, J. (2024). The brief mind wandering three-factor scale (BMW-3). Behavior Research Methods, 56(8), 8720–8744. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6

During the first weeks of term, during the lab session you worked with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering carried out by Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024). They created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens.

Examples of papers on measuring aspects of screen time
In addition to the paper by Kaye et al. (2020) referred to in the section with key readings (Section 2), the following papers are good examples of papers that focus on a specific aspect of screen time.
Baumgartner, S. E., Lemmens, J. S., Weeda, W. D., & Huizinga, M. (2017). Measuring media multitasking: Development of a short measure of media multitasking for adolescents. Journal of Media Psychology, 29(4), 188–197. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-1105/a000167

Baumgartner et al. (2017) developed a short media multitasking measure (MMM-S) – measuring the simultaneous use of two or more media.

Du, J., van Koningsbruggen, G. M., & Kerkhof, P. (2018). A brief measure of social media self-control failure. Computers in Human Behavior, 84, 68–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2018.02.002

Du et al. (2018) developed a 3-item scale, the Social Media Self-Control Failure (SMSCF) scale, to measure how often people give in to social media temptations.

Marty-Dugas, J., Ralph, B. C., Oakman, J. M., & Smilek, D. (2018). The relation between smartphone use and everyday inattention. Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice, 5(1), 46. https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cns0000131

Marty-Dugas et al. (2018) developed two different measures of smartphone use (general and absent-minded) and explore relationships with measures of everyday inattention.

Ohme, J., Araujo, T., de Vreese, C. H., & Piotrowski, J. T. (2021). Mobile data donations: Assessing self-report accuracy and sample biases with the iOS Screen Time function. Mobile Media & Communication, 9(2), 293-313.

Ohme et al. (2021) present a new methodological approach: mobile data donations using screenshots of the iOS Screen Time function. They assesses its feasibility, sample biases, and the accuracy of self-reported smartphone usage compared to log data in a general population sample of Dutch citizens.

Lab activity 1: Assumptions of Correlation Analysis

Question 1: Types of variables
Correlation would be an appropriate form of analysis for researchers interested in the relationship between:

Dog (breed) and height (cm) of owner
Speed of swimming (mph) and area of tank (cm)
Number of cows sitting and rain fall (mm)

Tip



For Pearson’s r, we hope the data look like a smooth, oval cloud: a straight-line relationship, equal spread of Y at every value of X, and a bell shape. We also watch for outliers: participants who don’t fit the overall pattern.
For each question below, look at the three plots (a histogram of X, a histogram of Y, and a scatterplot) and answer the questions. All the data are simulated for teaching.




Question 2: Revision and exam marks
Forty students reported how many hours per week they spent revising and then sat an exam.


Look at the two histograms only. Does any student look unusual? Note anything you see.
Now look at the scatterplot. Which students do not fit the overall pattern? Describe each one, giving their approximate revision hours and exam mark.
Why can the scatterplot reveal something the histograms cannot?
Before running any analysis, what should you check about these students? Give two possible explanations for their scores.
If you calculated Pearson’s r for all 40 students, and then again without these students, would r get higher, lower or stay the same? Explain your reasoning.



Question 3: Arousal and task performance
Sixty participants completed a memory task. Before the task, each was given a score for how aroused (alert and activated) they felt.


Describe the relationship between arousal and performance in words.
Look at the histograms. Do they suggest any problem with using Pearson’s r?
Without calculating anything, would you expect Pearson’s r to be strong and positive, strong and negative, or close to zero? Explain why.
Which assumption is violated here? Would switching to Spearman’s rho solve the problem? Why or why not?
What does this example tell you about reporting a correlation coefficient without looking at the scatterplot?



Question 4: Age and vocabulary
Eighty children aged between 6 and 16 took a vocabulary test.


Compare the spread of vocabulary scores for children aged about 7 to 8 with those aged about 13 to 15. Give approximate ranges for each group.
Which assumption is violated? Name it and describe what is wrong in your own words.
Could you have spotted this problem from the two histograms alone? Explain.
Why might this problem affect the p-value for Pearson’s r?
The spread of vocabulary scores grows roughly in proportion to the average score. Suggest one thing you could try.



Question 5: Reaction time and social media use
Eighty participants completed a reaction-time task and reported how many hours per week they spend on social media. Figure 4a shows the raw data.



Figure 5a. Raw data.



Describe the shape of each histogram.
Does the scatterplot look like an oval, bell-shaped cloud? Which assumption(s) appear to be violated?
In the lecture simulations, what happened to the false-positive rate when variables were skewed but unrelated? What would you still want to check in the scatterplot?

Figure 4b shows the same data after taking the natural log of both variables. Transforming the the data in this way is common approach for heavily skewed data.



Figure 5b. The same data on a log scale.



What has changed? Has the transformation solved every problem?
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of log-transforming the data.

Step 3: Check for missing data
We can check whether there are any missing data in a data-frame in multiple ways:

Lab activity 4: Outliers

Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Read in the data file
Build scatterplots with geom_point(), and add a line of best fit using geom_smooth()
Remove outliers using filter(), and create another scatterplot
Calculate and interpret Pearson’s r using correlation() for data with and without outlier values



Step 1: Read in the data file
For this lab activity, you’ll need the file named revision_exam.csv.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use read_csv() to read in the data file named revision_exam.csv; tell R where to find the file and what it is called. Make sure you’ve run the code chunk. Then, check that you can see the ‘object’ (also called ‘data-frame’) in the Environment (top right quadrant) for the file you read in.



Step 2: Build a scatterplot
Now we are ready to build a scatterplot to visualise the relationship between two of the variables. We are going to look at the relationship between revision time and exam marks.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use ggplot() to tell R what data to plot and which variables tot use. Then, add layers to plot the datapoints (use geom_point()) and the line of best fit (use geom_smooth(method="lm", se=TRUE)). If you need more guidance on how to do this, look at the Hint below. If you are still stuck, you can look at the Code below.







Hint





Use the function ggplot(). Start by writing ggplot() on the next line of the code chunk. Inside the ggplot() function, we need to tell R which data-frame (data=) and which variables to use (mapping=aes(x= , y= ))).
Then, we need to tell R what type of plot we want. We do this by adding a + to the line on which you’ve written ggplot(), then on the next line you add a ‘geometric object’, in this case geom_point().
We also want to add a line of best fit. We do this by adding a + to the line on which you’ve written geom_point(), then on the next line you add another ‘geometric object’, in this case geom_smooth(). We want to specify what type of line of best fit, we do this by adding method="lm", se=TRUE inside the brackets of geom_smooth().
This will give you a basic scatterplot. Revisit the lab activity code from week 1 to remind yourself how to change any of the features (such as the colour, the background, add titles to the axes etc.).









Code





ggplot(data = data_revision_exam, mapping = aes(x=revision_hours, y=exam_mark)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se=TRUE)





Step 3: Remove outliers using filter(), and create another scatterplot
Now,we’ll remove the two participants with outlier values. We’ll do this using the filter() function from the dplyr package (part of the tidyverse).






How does filter() work?



The filter() function allows you to select specific rows from a data frame based on one or more conditions.
For example, imagine we have a dataset containing information about participants in a psychology study, including their age and gender. We might want to select only participants who are over 18 years old.
We can do this using:
filter(data, age > 18)
Here: - data is the name of our data frame. - age > 18 is the condition we want to apply. - note these two bits of information are separated within the function by a comma. - only rows where the condition is TRUE are kept.
We can also apply multiple conditions. For example, to select participants who are over 18 and identify as a woman:
filter(data, age > 18, gender == "Woman")
When we provide multiple conditions separated by commas, filter() keeps only rows that satisfy all of the conditions.
Some useful operators for filtering data include:



Operator
Meaning
Example




==
Equal to
gender == "Woman"


!=
Not equal to
gender != "Woman"


>
Greater than
age > 18


<
Less than
age < 30


>=
Greater than or equal to
age >= 18


<=
Less than or equal to
age <= 30



We can also use & (AND) and | (OR) to combine conditions.
For example:
filter(data, age >= 18 & age <= 30)
This selects participants aged between 18 and 30 (inclusive).



Action: Use filter() to remove the two participants with outlier values. We can do this by specifying that we only want to keep data from participants who revised for more than 5, but less than 25 hours. The code on the handbook page does this. You can copy the code into your script. Please have a close look and, using the information above, make sure you understand what each part of the code does.

data_revision_exam_clean <- filter(data_revision_exam, revision_hours >5 & revision_hours < 25 )

Make sure to use data_revison_exam_clean. Then, add layers to plot the datapoints (use geom_point()) and the line of best fit (use geom_smooth(method="lm", se=TRUE)).

Questions Step 3

Looking at the line of best fit in the first scatterplot (which included the participants with outlier values), how would you describe the relationship between revision hours and exam mark?
What do you estimate the value of the correlation coefficient to be?
Looking at the line of best fit in the second scatterplot (without the participants with outlier values), how would you describe the relationship between revision hours and exam mark now?
What do you estimate the value of the correlation coefficient to be now?



Step 4: Calculate and interpret Pearson’s r using correlation() for data with and without outlier values

Action: Run two correlation analyses: one with the data with (data_revision_exam) and one with the data without (data_revision_exam_clean) outlier values. If you can’t remember how to do this, look at the Hint below. Give it a go. If you are still stuck, look at the code you wrote for Lab activity 3, Step 3.







Hint





Use the correlation() function we used last week. You need to specify the following information inside the correlation() function:

data: data = data_revision_exam
variables: select = c(“revision_hours”, “exam_mark”)
method = “pearson”
p_adjust = “none”







Lab activity 5: Spearman’s rho

Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Read in the data file
Build a scatterplot with geom_point(), and add a line of best fit using geom_smooth()
Calculate and interpret Pearson’s r and Spearman’s rho using correlation()



Step 1: Read in the data file
For this lab activity, you’ll need the file named reading_enjoyment_books.csv. It contains data from sixty adults who were asked how much they enjoy reading (variable name = reading_enjoyment), on a single item from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much), and how many books they had read in the past 12 months (variable name = books_read).

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use read_csv() to read in the data file named reading_enjoyment_books.csv; tell R where to find the file and what it is called. Make sure you’ve run the code chunk. Then, check that you can see the ‘object’ (also called ‘data-frame’) in the Environment (top right quadrant) for the file you read in.



Step 2: Build a scatterplot using geom_jitter() instead of geom_point()
Now we are ready to build a scatterplot to visualise the relationship between reading enjoyment and number of books read.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use ggplot() to tell R what data to plot and which variables tot use. Then, add layers to plot the datapoints (use geom_point()) and the line of best fit (use geom_smooth(method="lm", se=TRUE)). If you need more guidance on how to do this, look at the Hint below. If you are still stuck, you can look at the code you wrote for Lab activity 4, Step 2.







Hint





Use the function ggplot(). Start by writing ggplot() on the next line of the code chunk. Inside the ggplot() function, we need to tell R which data-frame (data=) and which variables to use (mapping=aes(x= , y= ))).
Then, we need to tell R what type of plot we want. We do this by adding a + to the line on which you’ve written ggplot(), then on the next line you add a ‘geometric object’, in this case geom_point().
We also want to add a line of best fit. We do this by adding a + to the line on which you’ve written geom_point(), then on the next line you add another ‘geometric object’, in this case geom_smooth(). We want to specify what type of line of best fit, we do this by adding method="lm", se=TRUE inside the brackets of geom_smooth().
This will give you a basic scatterplot. Revisit the lab activity code from week 1 to remind yourself how to change any of the features (such as the colour, the background, add titles to the axes etc.).



Many of the participants gave the same rating and read the same number of books, so their points sit exactly on top of each other. geom_jitter() fixes this by moving each point a tiny random amount, so overlapping points spread out and you can see how many there are.






How does geom_jitter() work?



geom_jitter() moves each point a tiny random amount, so overlapping points spread out and you can see how many there are.
You can tell R how to jitter the data points:

width = 0.1 is the largest random nudge to the left or right. Ratings are whole numbers, so a point at 3 is moved to somewhere between 2.9 and 3.1. This is small enough that the five vertical stripes stay clearly separate.
height = 0 means the points are not moved up or down. The number of books is a real count, so nudging points vertically would make the plot show values that aren’t in the data.
alpha = 0.6 makes the points partly transparent (0 is invisible and 1 is solid). Where points overlap, the colour becomes darker, which gives a second clue about where the data are concentrated.

Jittering only changes how the plot looks. The data and the correlation are not affected.



Action: Instead of using geom_point() in the scatterplot, try geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.6).
